title: Twelve, a limp and knee pain: look at the hip
objective: Suspect slipped capital femoral epiphysis in a pre-teen or teen with hip, thigh or knee pain and a limp, since knee-only pain often delays diagnosis; obesity is the single biggest risk factor

brief.situation: 16:00 in an outpatient pediatric clinic. You are the physical therapist. Ethan, 12, comes with his mother. His pediatrician's referral: 'Left knee pain and limp for 3 weeks, likely patellofemoral pain or Osgood-Schlatter disease. Evaluate and treat.'
handover: No imaging has been done. He takes ibuprofen as needed.
His mother says the limp got worse after he slipped at recess yesterday, but he walked in.
Clinic policy: a suspected fracture or slipped growth plate goes to the children's hospital emergency department the same day, non-weight bearing; tell the referring pediatrician.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each part of the exam takes the time on its button. Decide what to examine, what it means and what to do.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Does Ethan have patellofemoral pain? What do you suspect, and what happens next?

parts.label: Suspicion
parts.criteria: A 12-year-old with knee and thigh pain, a limp, a normal knee exam, lost internal rotation with the thigh rolling outward on flexion, worse after a minor fall, and a BMI above the 95th percentile: suspected slipped capital femoral epiphysis, a hip problem felt in the knee.
parts.modelAnswer: Not patellofemoral pain. His knee is normal, but his left hip has lost internal rotation and rolls outward when flexed, which reproduces his pain. A 12-year-old with a limp, knee pain, a recent fall and a BMI over the 95th percentile has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis until X-rays say otherwise.

parts.label: Action
parts.criteria: No hop test, squats or treadmill; non-weight bearing now; same-day emergency department or orthopedic assessment with hip X-rays; tells the pediatrician.
parts.modelAnswer: No loading tests or exercise. Crutches or a wheelchair, no weight on the left leg, and send him to the children's emergency department today for hip X-rays and orthopedics. Then call his pediatrician.

expertPath.text: History: knee and inner-thigh ache, a limp, worse after a fall. Examine the knee: normal.
Examine the hip gently: no internal rotation, the thigh rolls outward on flexion. Check his BMI percentile: above the 95th.
Crutches, no weight on the left. Send him to the children's emergency department today for hip X-rays; tell the pediatrician.

unstable.headline: The slip became unstable
unstable.body: Loading a hip with a suspected slip can turn a stable slip into an unstable one. Examine the hip before any loading test, and stop weight bearing once you suspect it.

missedSlip.headline: The slip was missed
missedSlip.body: Knee pain with a normal knee in a pre-teen or teen is a hip problem until proven otherwise. Diagnosis is often delayed for weeks when only the knee is examined.

sameDay.headline: Suspected and sent the same day
sameDay.body: You examined the hip when the knee was normal, avoided loading, made him non-weight bearing and sent him for same-day X-rays and orthopedics. That is the expert path.

referredGaps.headline: Referred, with gaps
referredGaps.body: Check whether the hip was examined before any loading, whether he stopped bearing weight, and whether X-rays happened the same day.

time_up.headline: Still in the clinic
time_up.body: A suspected slip needs a decision in the same visit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Knee or distal thigh pain is the only complaint in a sizable share of slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and diagnosis is often delayed for weeks. A 12-year-old with a limp, knee pain, a normal knee examination, lost internal rotation with the thigh rolling outward on flexion and a BMI above the 95th percentile has a suspected slip. Loading tests and exercise risk worsening the slip; he should be non-weight bearing and assessed by orthopedics with hip X-rays the same day, and the referring pediatrician told.
